clue.text: Perhaps young ladies returning diamonds like waste from coal mine?

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters before it are read backwards

parts.note: EG, for example, is what 'perhaps' signals in crosswords
gals is informal for young women
D is the card-suit abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: A grim mining image: young women handing back diamonds that look like coal-mine waste.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'Perhaps young ladies' is turned round (EG GALS becomes SLAGGE); the diamonds' D is tacked on afterwards. EG = 'perhaps' is a standard crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Slag is the stony residue left after mining or smelting, so something covered in or resembling it can be described as slagged.

clue.text: Save seafood that's cold, not hot

indicators.note: 'this, not that' means one letter stands where the other used to be

parts.note: a shrimp is a small shellfish
C is the tap abbreviation for cold
H is the tap abbreviation for hot, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: A thrifty shopper rescuing some chilled seafood that has gone cold.
explanation.walkthrough: In the seafood word the H for hot is swapped for the C for cold.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrimp is to economise or skimp on spending, which is a way of saving money.

clue.text: Taking part in dry run for show

parts.note: to be at an event is to be taking part in it
a dry run is a trial or test

explanation.surface: A performer joining the rehearsal before a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like a theatrical noun, but it is a verb meaning to prove.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to bear witness to or demonstrate something, which is one sense of showing it to be true.

clue.text: Extremely grave old writer cracks systems for calculating lengths

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of grave
O is a standard abbreviation for old
the writer of the clue, the setter, refers to themself as me
has a crack at, that is, attempts

explanation.surface: A gloomy elderly author struggling to understand measuring systems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracks' looks like a container instruction but is simply a verb meaning has a go; the writer is the setter, ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Geometry is the branch of mathematics dealing with measurement of lines, angles and distances, and different geometries are different such frameworks.

clue.text: Bashful, perhaps, having served up some half-raw dinners

indicators.note: in a down clue, something served up is sent upwards, so it reads bottom to top
only a portion of the following words is taken, a run of consecutive letters

parts.note: a run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A shy person who has been served undercooked meals.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters FRAWD sit across 'half-raw dinners' and read upwards give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bashful is one of the seven little men in Snow White, so he is an example of the answer, flagged by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Old-fashioned craft which might help you shape hedges

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fast nineteenth-century sailing ship

definitions.text: which might help you shape hedges
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a cutting tool for trimming

explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' suggests a traditional skill such as topiary, but here it means a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a swift tall-masted sailing ship of the past and a pair of shears or trimmer used by gardeners.

clue.text: Church saint privy to wit — no point complaining about it

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
ST is the abbreviation for saint
a privy is a toilet, informally a lav
IE, id est, means that is or to wit

explanation.surface: A churchgoing saint who is in on the joke, telling everyone to stop grumbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Privy to' looks like 'in on the secret', but privy is the old outdoor toilet and 'to wit' is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase, literally 'that's life', is said with a shrug when something can't be helped, so complaining would be pointless.

clue.text: Today's crossword setter offers the same again

parts.note: the setter speaks of themself as I
to bid is to make an offer

explanation.surface: The day's puzzle compiler serving up a repeat of a previous offering.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is I, and 'offers' is a verb, giving I BID.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibid, short for Latin ibidem, is used in footnotes to cite the same source as the previous reference.

clue.text: Things on sleigh possibly dispatched in advance by one of the poles

parts.note: sent beforehand: PRE plus SENT
S for south, one of the two geographic poles

explanation.surface: Santa's cargo sent ahead from the North Pole before Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: The poles point to the North Pole and Santa, but the letter needed is S for the other one, south.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Christmas is pictured delivering gifts by sleigh, so wrapped gifts are an example of its load.

clue.text: Retired padre's losing head about barely revised versions

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so that letter is lost

parts.note: ret. is an abbreviation for retired

indicators.note: 'about' can mean turned around and rearranged, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: the chaplain's word PADRES with its first letter dropped

explanation.surface: A retired chaplain losing his mind over sermons that have barely been changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing head' sounds like going mad, but it removes the P of padre's before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A retread is a tyre given new tread, and figuratively a reworking of old material with only minor changes.

clue.text: Treacherous type regularly wanting in on correspondence

parts.note: a rat is a betrayer

indicators.note: letters missing at regular intervals means every other one is dropped

parts.note: the first and third letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A traitor desperate to be let in on someone's private letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correspondence' suggests letters, but it means a proportional relation between quantities.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio expresses how two quantities relate proportionally, which is a mathematical sense of correspondence.

clue.text: Sober sailors can essentially get any number a little tipsy

parts.note: ABs are able seamen
a tin is a can

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its heart, so the central letter is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of get
N stands for any number in maths

indicators.note: a small bit of a word is taken, just its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of tipsy

explanation.surface: Teetotal sailors can still get a bit drunk on any amount, an ironic picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about drinking, but each word yields a small piece; AB (able seaman) and N for an unspecified number are conventions.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who abstains from alcohol stays clear-headed, so this adjective is a close synonym for not drinking.

clue.text: Old lady's emotional, missing ace showing dominance

parts.note: old lady is slang for mother, MA, with the possessive S

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so a letter is taken out

parts.note: tearful means emotional, close to crying
A is the abbreviation for ace, the letter removed

explanation.surface: An elderly woman upset at losing her winning card in a power game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' is British slang for one's mother, MA; the A is removed from the tearful word.
explanation.definitionFit: Masterful describes someone commanding and in control, which is exactly how a person asserting authority appears.

clue.text: Church event's cost covering base for font

indicators.note: to cover is to wrap round, so one piece sits outside another

parts.note: a fee is a charge or cost

indicators.note: in an across clue the base of a word is its end, so the last letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of font

explanation.surface: Money raised at a parish event pays for the base of the baptismal font.
explanation.walkthrough: The church font suggests a christening, but it is simply the word supplying its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fete is an outdoor fundraising fair, often held by a parish church with stalls and games.

clue.text: Philistine in uniform shortly denudes ground home to kitty

indicators.note: cutting a word short removes its final letter
a home houses its occupant, so one piece goes inside another
something ground is crushed and broken up, so its letters are mixed

parts.note: U is uniform in the NATO alphabet
the verb with its last letter cut
a kitty is a cat

explanation.surface: A boorish soldier in uniform stripping bare a patch of land where a cat lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a noun for land, but it is the past tense of grind; 'kitty' could be a money pool, but it is the cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A philistine is someone hostile or indifferent to culture and learning, so lacking schooling or refinement fits.

clue.text: Invigorated once more, enter 'DEJA VU' in a puzzle?

indicators.note: a puzzle is a state of confusion, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Writing the phrase for a sense of repetition into a crossword grid, feeling refreshed as if doing it again.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'once more' of the definition chimes with the repeated feeling of déjà vu in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To be rejuvenated is to be made young or lively again, so being re-energised is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Apple turnover used to feed this fussy person

parts.note: Steve Jobs co-founded Apple
a business's turnover is a measure of what it is worth

explanation.surface: An apple pastry served up to a picky eater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple turnover' is a pastry, but Apple is the company of Steve Jobs. A jobsworth is a British term for an official who hides behind petty rules ('more than my job's worth').
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang term describes a petty official who insists on rules to the letter, a nitpicking stickler.

clue.text: It cracks gemstone finally burnished on edge

indicators.note: something that cracks a shell breaks into it, ending up inside

parts.note: agate is a banded semi-precious stone
taken as written

indicators.note: at the finish of a word stands its last letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the final letter of burnished

explanation.surface: A gem cutter breaks a stone that has been polished at its rim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On edge' looks like part of the jeweller's scene, the polished rim, but it is the definition: nervous.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on edge means tense and nervous, the same restless anxiety as feeling agitated.

clue.text: A horse's boxing farmyard animal's ears and arse?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a nag is a horse, with the possessive S
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A horse lashing out at the head and rear of another farm animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an example: ears and arse use the same four letters rearranged; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Each word is a reordering of the other's letters, so the pair are examples of words formed by rearrangement.

clue.text: Posh bandmate reportedly produced sugary stuff

parts.note: Ginger Spice was a bandmate of Posh Spice in the Spice Girls

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so the sound is what counts

parts.note: produced as offspring, bred

explanation.surface: Gossip that one of Victoria Beckham's bandmates made something sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posh' looks like an adjective, but it is Posh Spice of the Spice Girls, whose bandmates included Ginger Spice.
explanation.definitionFit: Gingerbread is a sweet cake or biscuit flavoured with ginger and treacle, a sugary baked treat.

clue.text: Fruit tart contains trace of nuts — Methuselah ultimately leaves it

indicators.note: to leave is to depart, so a letter goes away
what contains something holds it inside

parts.note: a quiche is a savoury tart

indicators.note: a trace is the smallest hint, just the opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of nuts

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so the final letter is meant

parts.note: the final letter of the setter's pseudonym, the letter dropped

explanation.surface: The setter declines a fruit tart because it might hold nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit tart' wants to be one thing, but the fruit is the definition and the tart is QUICHE; Methuselah is this puzzle's setter.
explanation.definitionFit: The quince is a hard, aromatic pear-shaped fruit often cooked into jelly or paste.

clue.text: Be frugal with every last bit of useable stock made available

indicators.note: the last bit of each word is its final letter, taken from each in turn

parts.note: the final letters of these three words
a product that is out has been released and can be had

explanation.surface: Advice to use up every scrap of supplies on hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Every last bit' sounds like thrift talk, but it picks the final letter of the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out supplies is to make them last by using them sparingly, the essence of thrift.

clue.text: You shouldn't have to bedeck outsiders in off-the-peg garment

indicators.note: to bedeck is to adorn by wrapping around, so one piece sits outside the other

parts.note: said on receiving a gift, a thanks; ta is British for thank you

indicators.note: the outsiders of a word are its outer letters, the only ones kept

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone protesting they need not dress up strangers in ready-made clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You shouldn't have' is what people say when given a present, and 'ta' is British informal for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: The toga is the loose draped outer robe worn by citizens of ancient Rome, a type of clothing.

clue.text: Groundhog Day shown in attempt to endear cast

parts.note: to woo is to try to win affection
D is the abbreviation for day
to cast is to throw or chuck

explanation.surface: The film Groundhog Day, with its actors trying to charm the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic title asks to be read as one film, but it splits: the animal is the definition and Day gives D; 'cast' is a verb, not the actors.
explanation.definitionFit: The groundhog and woodchuck are two names for the same North American burrowing marmot.

clue.text: Baked loaves after scrapping starter of Easter eggs?

indicators.note: something baked has been cooked and transformed, so its letters are reworked
scrapping something throws it away, so a letter is removed first

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so only the initial letter is meant

parts.note: the first letter of Easter, the one dropped

explanation.surface: Bread baked for the holiday without the usual Easter eggs to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: Easter eggs look like one item, but Easter only gives its E to be removed and 'eggs?' is the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggs have a rounded elongated outline, so they are examples of that shape, which the question mark signals.

clue.text: Where sewer keeps things in perpetuity

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the next word, sitting within its letters

parts.note: the four letters in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: Where a drain stores things for ever, a deliberately odd image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' reads as a drain, but it is one who sews. An etui is a small ornamental case for needles and thread.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small decorative case for holding needles, thread and similar items, the kind a needleworker carries.

clue.text: Riot at art nouveau restaurant

indicators.note: nouveau is French for new, so the letters take a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Chaos breaking out at an eatery decorated in the Art Nouveau style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Art nouveau' reads as the design movement, but art belongs with the fodder and nouveau is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A trattoria is an informal Italian eating house, a kind of simple family-run dining establishment.

clue.text: Move with beat … it takes two

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
a go is a move or turn

explanation.surface: Dancing to the rhythm, which needs a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes the saying 'it takes two to tango'; 'beat' looks musical but means thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says it takes two to tango, so the partnered Argentine dance is what the phrase completes.

clue.text: Attractive person with little quirk penned one third of a sestet?

indicators.note: to be penned is to be shut in an enclosure, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a dish is slang for a good-looking person
a tic is a small habitual twitch or quirk

explanation.surface: A good-looking poet with a small eccentricity who wrote part of a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penned' suggests writing, but it means enclosed. A sestet is a six-line stanza, so a third of it is two lines.
explanation.definitionFit: A distich is a pair of verse lines, a couplet; three such pairs make up a six-line stanza.

clue.text: On vacation, drenched awnings turned European street most miserable

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so it is read backwards
vacating means emptying out, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters
the first and last letters
E is the abbreviation for European
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A rain-soaked holiday on a European street, with dripping awnings, makes for misery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' sounds like a holiday, but it empties the next words of their middles.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddest is the superlative of sad, and miserable means deeply unhappy, so the superlatives match.
